Operate CALIBER

Reference profile recovery runbook

What to do, and what never to do, when a reference-profile deployment stops halfway: owner failover, an unknown effect, a redelivered callback, an outbox backlog, a failed run with an effect in doubt.

OperatorRunbookBETA
PrerequisitesA CALIBER deployment running the reference profile · An operator-scoped token, and an admin-scoped one for the legacy effect resolve · Read access to the CALIBER database for the read-only queries
Reviewed 2026-10-28 · current main branch docs contract

Use this page when something in a reference-profile deployment stopped halfway: the process that was running the background loops died, an external effect has no recorded outcome, a callback or webhook arrived twice, events are not being delivered, or a run ended failed with an effect in doubt. Each section says what the failure looks like, how to tell, what is safe to do, and what is never safe.

It collects what Reference profile and ADR 0002 explain in pieces, and it adds no behavior: every state, code and endpoint below is the one the code uses, and the scenarios V07 (a dispatcher killed at any moment), V08 (a timeout) and V09 (outbox and inbox) in caliber/tests/egi_scenarios/ exercise the effect and event paths end to end. The older Operations runbook covers recoveries that do not depend on the lease (releases, queues, rollbacks) and is still the page for those.

All HTTP paths are relative to /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber; this page writes them as /caliber/....

What is wired today#

Read this first: it decides which sections you will meet in practice.

PieceOn mainWhat it means for you
Execution-owner lease, failover, execution_role in readinessmerged (B13.2, B13.3)Failover below applies as written
Outbox, inbox, process_oncemerged (B13.4, B13.5a)Backlog and redelivery sections apply as written
Receipt callbackmerged (B05.4b, B13.5b)The one consumer of the inbound inbox
Effect proposals, receipts, reconciler, operator viewmerged as modules and a read-only view (B05.1 to B05.6)Rows appear in the view only once something writes proposals
The dispatcher that dispatches proposalsmerged (B04.1, #724); a manifest-backed webhook or API-request node dispatches through it only when its run supplies a governed effect context (B04.2), and no production worker builds that context yetA real run's effects still go through the legacy effect ledger; proposal rows appear only where something supplies that context
The owner loop that runs the reconciler, and the rule for a dispatch stuck under the current leasemerged (B05.5d, #997): EffectReconcilerTask, reference profile, on by default (CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_ENABLED)Every CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_INTERVAL_SECONDS (15 s) the owner asks about unknown and abandoned effects by key, and a dispatch left under the current lease longer than CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS (15 min) becomes unknown
An audited operator action for a proposalmerged (B05.5d, #997): reconcile and nothing elseAsks the downstream now, as the owner, and records who asked and why. It never records what you believe: see What you can do that is safe
Parking a gated run and resuming it after reconciliationmerged (B05.5c, #996)A gated run is durably waiting_effect; authoritative settlement wakes the same run from its checkpoint

So today the effect you will actually meet is a legacy ledger claim (caliber_effect_ledger, status in_progress); the proposal states below are what the same procedures become when the dispatcher lands, and they are written down now so that the first unknown proposal is not the first time anyone reads them.

Rules that never bend#

  1. Never send a dispatched effect again by hand, and never re-run something to "make it go through". A dispatched effect may already have happened. The only way back from unknown is a question to the downstream by the original key (there is no transition from unknown to dispatched).
  2. Never mark an effect failed, skipped or reconciled without the downstream's own evidence. The platform records failed for an unknown effect only by moving it through reconciled first, and only when the connector proves absence final (absence_proven); a definitive rejection is recorded failed only from dispatched, on the first and only dispatch. A missing record is delayed visibility until proven otherwise. For a legacy claim, skip and retry are statements about the outside world: make them only after you looked at the remote system.
  3. Never edit or delete ledger, proposal, receipt, manifest, outbox or inbox rows. They are the evidence. On PostgreSQL the immutable tables refuse it; on SQLite (development only) they do not, which is a reason to stay off it, not a way around.
  4. Never edit a shipped migration, and never downgrade the schema to fix a stuck row: a downgrade drops tables together with their rows (0116 drops caliber_execution_owner, 0119 the outbox and its inbox, 0122 the inbound inbox, 0123 the proposals, 0125 the receipts; 0126 and 0127 drop the dispatch token and the approval binding columns), and the evidence goes with them. Schema changes are a new revision.
  5. Never start a second owner by hand. Do not write the caliber_execution_owner row and do not run loops outside the lease. A secondary acquires the lease by itself when the old one lapses.
  6. Capture before you act. Save the output of the first-look commands below with the time; a restart destroys some of it.

First look#

# Is this replica ready, which profile is it under, and is it the owner or a secondary? (the body is wrapped in "data")
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/readiness" | jq '.data | {ready, profile, execution_role}'

# Is the workflow-run queue draining, and are workers alive?
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/queue"

# Effects that need a person: legacy ledger claims and effect proposals, labelled apart
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/effects"

# Outbound webhooks that were never delivered
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/webhook-dead-letters"

The readiness body (under data; curl does not unwrap it, and neither does it unwrap the 2xx answers of the callback) carries profile and execution_role. Ask every replica: exactly one should answer owner and the rest secondary. The lease owner's id is host:pid:random, one per process incarnation, so it names the machine that holds it. The read-only queries used below (PostgreSQL; expires_at is naive UTC database time):

-- the execution-owner lease: who holds it, which fencing token, when it lapses, and whether it already has
SELECT lease_name, owner_id, fencing_token, acquired_at, renewed_at, expires_at,
       expires_at <= timezone('utc', clock_timestamp()) AS lapsed
FROM caliber_execution_owner;

-- outbox depth: pending, delivered and dead rows
SELECT status, count(*) AS n, min(created_at) AS oldest FROM caliber_event_outbox GROUP BY status;

-- outbox rows that ran out of attempts, with the consumer and exception class that failed (never a payload)
SELECT event_id, event_type, attempts, last_error, created_at
FROM caliber_event_outbox WHERE status = 'dead' ORDER BY created_at;

-- inbound inbox reservations that never reached processed
SELECT consumer, source, event_id, status, received_at FROM caliber_inbox_events WHERE status = 'received';

Owner crash and failover#

What it looks like. The process holding the lease was killed, lost its database, or hung. Loops stop; runs that were running sit until their own lease lapses; /readiness on the survivors still says secondary for up to one lease.

How the takeover works. The lease (caliber_execution_owner) expires by the database's clock, so a paused or skewed process cannot keep it. A secondary tries to acquire every CALIBER_EXECUTION_LEASE_SECONDS / 3 (default lease 30 s, minimum 3 s). When it wins, the fencing token grows by exactly one, it starts the loops and /readiness says owner. The takeover scenario (V14) asserts that it happens within twice the lease, SIGKILL included. An owner that cannot renew, or cannot reach the database, stops its own loops after two thirds of the lease and reports secondary: losing the lease fails closed.

Steps.

  1. Read the lease row (query above) and /readiness on every replica. Note fencing_token and expires_at. The process logs (caliber.execution_role) say execution-owner lease acquired (owner=... token=N) on a takeover and execution-owner lease lost (...); stopping the owner-only loops on a loss; grep them to see a failover.
  2. If the holder is dead and expires_at is in the past or within one lease: wait one lease plus a tick and read again. fencing_token should have grown by one and exactly one replica should say owner. Do nothing else.
  3. After the takeover, work left behind is picked up by the loops themselves, each by its own rule. The per-loop table is Recovery by stage in ADR 0002; the ones you will notice:
    Left behindWhat happensWhen
    A workflow run runningrequeued (error_code lease_recovered, event workflow.run.recovered) and run again from the beginning, unless its summary already carries a resume checkpoint (then from that same checkpoint); a run parked at an approval or wait is not running and is never recovered this waywhen its run lease lapses (CALIBER_WORKFLOW_RUN_LEASE_SECONDS, 60 s)
    Webhooks accepted but not deliveredbecome dead letters of kind shutdown; replay them (below)when their accept lease lapses (at least 60 s)
    Outbox rows claimed by the dead publisherdelivered again by the new publisher; the consumer's inbox drops a repeatat lease expiry (30 s)
    A refinement job runningmarked failed by the janitor, not requeuedheartbeat older than CALIBER_JANITOR_STALE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS (300 s)
    A calibration job runningnothing, on purpose: abandon it or submit a new linked jobsee P4
    A workspace import runningmoved to reconcile_required (not retryable; queue a new import job for the same content, which is safe by digest)after CALIBER_WORKSPACE_IMPORT_LEASE_SECONDS (300 s)
    An effect dispatched under the old leasebecomes abandoned; see the next sectiononce the new owner holds a higher token
  1. A recovered run is not a safe run. It starts again from the beginning. Only webhook and API-request nodes go through the effect ledger: an effect of those nodes that it already claimed is not repeated (the ledger replays it, or reports the claim indeterminate). Effects of other nodes (MCP tools, OpenAPI tools, knowledge builds, output buckets) are not ledgered and can happen again. Before you let a recovered run proceed, or retry it, read its workflow.run.recovered event and check the downstream for any non-ledgered effect it could already have made.

No owner after two leases. Every process is a secondary when the lease store is unreachable (the lease calls fail closed and /readiness reports the database), or when the loops fail to start after an acquisition (the error is logged by caliber.execution_role, the lease is released and the next tick tries again). Fix the cause (the database, the failing loop); do not try to force an owner.

Two replicas say owner. This must not persist. The loops are not yet fenced per transition, so after a lease loss the old owner may finish the transition it was in, bounded by CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS (30 s): read /readiness again after that long. If two replicas still both say owner, stop one and treat it as an incident: capture both readiness bodies and the lease row first. SQLite gives no fencing guarantee at all and the reference profile refuses it.

Clean restart. A deliberate shutdown stops the loops while it keeps renewing the lease, then releases it, so the successor starts without waiting for expiry. A rolling deploy therefore hands over cleanly; a SIGKILL costs one lease.

Never. Do not shorten the wait by writing the lease row, by restarting the survivors "to make one win", or by re-running the work the dead owner was doing.

A stuck or unknown effect#

An effect is stuck when nobody has the final word on whether it reached the downstream. Two records exist and the view never mixes them (source and safe_actions on every row):

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" \
  "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/effects?source=proposal&proposal_state=open&limit=100"
from caliber_sdk import CaliberClient

client = CaliberClient()  # CALIBER_BASE_URL and CALIBER_TOKEN come from the environment
view = client.system.effects(source="proposal", proposal_state="unknown")
for row in view["proposals"]:
    print(row["proposal_id"], row["state"], row["reason"], row["abandoned"], row["blocks_dependents"])
print(view["lease"])  # the stored execution-owner lease (also returned when source is "all"), or None

A proposal (source: effect_proposal)#

States: proposed, approved, dispatched, committed, failed, unknown, reconciled. The open ones, which block what depends on them, are dispatched, unknown and reconciled.

You seeIt meansDo
dispatched, abandoned: truethe lease that dispatched it was replaced; the attempt may have been sentNothing by hand. The new owner's next loop pass (within CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_INTERVAL_SECONDS, 15 s) records unknown (abandoned_dispatch) and asks the downstream by key; it keeps blocking its dependents until that settles
dispatched, abandoned: falsethe dispatcher's own attempt in flight, or its lease lapsed and nobody has taken over yetRead lease in the same response: expired: true means failover has not completed, go to Owner crash. Otherwise wait: a dispatcher whose settle fails records unknown itself, and the loop moves a row that is still dispatched after CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS (see below)
dispatched, abandoned: nullno recorded token or no lease to compareTreat as unknown; never abandon it by hand
unknownno recorded outcome (a timeout after the send, an ambiguous answer, a failed settle, an abandoned or expired dispatch)Wait for the loop (every 15 s) or a verified callback, or ask now with reconcile. It is never sent again. reason says why: ambiguous:<code>, receipt_unverified, settle_failed:<code or exception class>, abandoned_dispatch, in_flight_expired
reconciledthe reconciler began settling it and has not finishedWait; the next pass or the callback finishes it
committeda verified receipt existsDo not repeat it. (The platform makes at most one local claim per effect and verifies a receipt; it does not promise exactly-once delivery by the downstream)
faileda definitive rejection, not sent, or proven absenceFinal. A new run is a new effect

How an unknown effect gets settled. Only the owner's reconciler asks, by the original logical key, through the connector's own lookup, at the base_url of the CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS binding for that connector and project. What comes back:

The downstream saysResult
a stored request that is this proposal's effectverified receipt, committed
404 from a connector that proves absence finalfailed (absence_proven)
404 from any other connector (document-request included)still unknown: delayed visibility or a request still in flight
5xx, 401 or any other statusstill unknown (detail http_<code>)
a 2xx whose body is not this proposal's effect (unreadable, or another request under the key)still unknown, reported unverified
cannot be reached, or no binding for the connector and projectstill unknown (lookup_failed, not_bound)

A dispatched row that does not clear. A row with abandoned: false and lease.expired: false was dispatched under the lease the owner still holds. If the dispatcher's settle fails while it keeps that lease (the store went away after the send, the receipt lookup raised), the dispatcher records unknown itself (settle_failed:<code>), so such a row does not stay dispatched. If it could not even do that (the store was still down, the thread died), the owner loop moves the row to unknown (in_flight_expired, audited as effect_in_flight_expired) once it has been dispatched for longer than CALIBER_EFFECT_IN_FLIGHT_MAX_SECONDS (900 s by default) and asks the downstream by key in the same pass. Neither rule sends anything. A row that is older than that bound and still dispatched means the loop is not running (the process is a secondary, or CALIBER_EFFECT_RECONCILER_ENABLED=false, or the loop is failing: its heartbeat row has kind effect_reconciler): check /readiness execution_role and the owner's logs. Do not resend. Capture the row (proposal_id, logical_key, owner_id, dispatch_token, dispatched_at) and the lease, ask the downstream by key, and escalate.

When to wait, and for how long. An unknown that survives a pass is not an error: a request that is still in flight, or a read that does not yet see its own write, looks exactly like a request that never arrived. Wait while the downstream's own people can still say it may land. The V07 scenario shows the case: a dispatcher killed before the send leaves the effect unknown, the reconciler's lookup finds nothing, and only when the request lands late from elsewhere does the next pass commit it, with the downstream counting one mutation throughout.

What you can do that is safe.

  • Ask the downstream's owner whether the request exists, by the proposal's logical_key (the idempotency key, in the view). That is evidence; keep it with the incident.
  • Ask the platform to ask the downstream now (admin scope, audited). The loop already does this every pass; this is for when you have just learned the request is visible and do not want to wait. It is the only action the view offers for a proposal (safe_actions: ["reconcile"], on an unknown or reconciled row and on a dispatched row that is abandoned: true):
      curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"reason": "INC-4471: the downstream owner confirms the request is visible"}' \
    "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/effects/proposals/$PROPOSAL_ID/reconcile"

    The body is reason (1 to 500 characters) and nothing else: any other key is 400, because there is nothing an operator can assert. Read outcome and state in the answer. committed means the downstream showed the request and the platform recorded a verified receipt. unknown (with http_404, http_5xx, unverified, lookup_failed or not_bound) means the evidence is not enough and nothing changed: a 404 is never read as "it did not happen". in_flight means the row is the dispatcher's own attempt and is still younger than the bound. Every request leaves one effect_reconcile_requested audit row (who, why, outcome, state afterwards) whether or not the proposal moved. It runs under the lease of the process that serves the request. A secondary answers 409 not_execution_owner: ask the owner (/readiness shows which role a process has, and lease in the view names the owner). A lease taken over mid-request is 409 lease_lost with nothing recorded; a settled or never-dispatched proposal is 409 not_reconcilable; more than 4 requests in flight in one process get 429 (retry shortly). A failed request is audited too, by error code or exception class only.

  • Ask the connector to redeliver its receipt callback (see Callback and webhook redelivery). The platform asks the downstream itself before it records anything, so a callback can only confirm what the downstream confirms.
  • Nothing else. Do not acquire the lease yourself to call the reconciler (see Reconciler).

An effect that stays unknown for good. There is deliberately no operator action that marks a proposal committed or failed on your say-so. A proposal becomes committed only with a receipt the platform read back from the downstream by key, and failed only when the connector proves absence final; marking it failed on a belief would unblock everything that depends on it while the effect may in fact have happened (the legacy ledger's resolve does take your word, a proposal never does). What that means in practice: a downstream that cannot yet show the request (a 404 is delayed visibility as far as anyone can tell) leaves the proposal unknown and its dependents blocked, and every later pass and reconcile asks again until the downstream shows it, or its owner redelivers the receipt callback. A connector with no lookup by key bound for the project (not_bound, which is every http connector proposal today: a generic webhook or API request has no read-by-key contract) cannot be settled by the platform at all; confirm what happened with the downstream's owner, keep that evidence with the incident, leave the row and its parked run as they are, and escalate: the follow-up is a connector with a lookup, not an override.

What is never safe. Re-sending the request; creating the same effect from a new run; editing the proposal row; deleting it; moving it with SQL. There is no operator action that fails an unknown proposal without the downstream's evidence, by design.

A legacy ledger claim (source: legacy_ledger)#

The queued-run worker claims caliber_effect_ledger before an effectful node performs its effect. A claim that stays in_progress after a crash means the process died between the claim and the recorded outcome, or the request timed out after it may have left: whether it reached the remote system is unknown.

  1. List: GET /caliber/system/effects (defaults to status=in_progress). Note the effect_key, workflow_run_id and node_id.
  2. Decide at the remote system whether the effect happened. Do not infer it from CALIBER.
  3. Record the decision (admin scope, audited): POST /caliber/system/effects/{effect_key}/resolve.
       curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALIBER_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"resolution": "skip", "reason": "request id 8841 exists at the downstream"}' \
     "$CALIBER_BASE_URL/ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/system/effects/$EFFECT_KEY/resolve"

    skip (the effect did happen) marks the row completed: a later attempt of the same run replays it and does not repeat it. retry (it did not) marks the row failed, which a later attempt of the same run may claim again. A row that is not in_progress is refused (400), and so is an unknown key and any other resolution.

  4. The decision is on the row and in the audit log. It does not restart a run: see the next section.

Apply a proposal's key to the legacy resolve endpoint and it is refused (400) and changes nothing.

A gated, parked, or failed run#

What it looks like. A proposal-gated run is waiting_effect, with error_code=effect_reconciliation, a current node, and a resume_checkpoint_id in its summary. The checkpoint kind is effect_reconciliation; it records the node inputs and each unresolved proposal's id, state, logical key and intent digest. The operator view lists the same run in parked_runs, including reason=effect_dependency_unresolved and resume_policy=same_run_same_occurrence. A legacy-claim refusal remains a terminal failure whose message names the resolve endpoint.

Why. Before every node, at the top of every retry attempt, the runtime checks the effects the node and everything it depends on asked for. While one is dispatched, unknown or reconciled, the node does not run and nothing absorbs the refusal: no fan-out item, loop iteration or error boundary turns it into a handled error. This is the guarantee, not a fault: no write that depends on an effect nobody can vouch for is made.

A parked run is not manually resumed. While waiting_effect, POST /caliber/workflow-runs/{run_id}/resume and retry are refused. The reconciler or a verified receipt callback is the only wake-up path. When every checkpointed proposal reaches committed or failed, the platform changes the same run to queued, emits workflow.run.effect_resumed, and the worker resumes from the checkpoint. The run id, logical key and intent digest remain unchanged, so no second logical occurrence or mutation is created. A run that is genuinely failed remains terminal: no transition leaves it, and retry creates a new run.

Steps.

  1. Find the run in parked_runs (or find its proposal in the view above, using the workflow_run_id filter) and inspect its checkpoint reason and effect states.
  2. Do not call resume or retry while it is waiting_effect; settle each proposal by the reconciler or a verified callback.
  3. Wait for workflow.run.effect_resumed and the run to return to queued. The worker then uses the stored checkpoint and preserves the original occurrence.
  4. If the run is genuinely terminal failed, settle the effect first and only then decide about a retry, with the owner of the downstream:
    • effect committed (or legacy skip): the work is done. Do not retry the run; if later nodes must still run, that is a design question for the workflow owner, not a button.
    • effect failed with proof (or legacy retry): a retry is safe with respect to this effect.
    • effect still unknown: do not retry. A retry would ask for the effect again.
  5. A run that lease recovery requeued runs again from the beginning. If an effect it claimed is still in_progress (or a proposal of it is open), it ends failed at that node; it needs no manual retry, and a manual retry does not help it (that is a new run, see above). Read its workflow.run.recovered event (GET /caliber/workflow-runs/{run_id}/events) and apply step 3 before anything else.

Never. Retry the run "to see whether it works now" while its effect is open.

A governed step refused for its token budget, or left a reservation open#

What it looks like. A run failed with governed agent step token reservation refused: token_budget_exhausted (budget=B committed=C requested=R), or ... reservation_replayed, or ... store_failed; or a row of caliber_step_token_reservations that stays reserved after its step should have ended.

-- what a run has counted: an open reservation counts at its whole ceiling, a final one at its charge
SELECT state, count(*) AS n, sum(coalesce(charged_tokens, reserved_tokens)) AS tokens
FROM caliber_step_token_reservations WHERE workflow_run_id = :run GROUP BY state;

-- open reservations past their deadline (the owner finalizes them after CALIBER_AGENT_RESERVATION_GRACE_SECONDS)
SELECT reservation_id, workflow_run_id, node_id, occurrence_id, attempt, reserved_tokens, deadline_at
FROM caliber_step_token_reservations WHERE state = 'reserved' AND deadline_at < now() ORDER BY deadline_at;

Why. A governed step reserves its max_tokens ceiling against the run's budget (CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS) before its adapter is called, and is charged what it reported only when the platform believes it; every other result keeps the whole reservation. This is the guarantee, not a fault: a call whose outcome nobody knows stays charged.

Steps.

  1. token_budget_exhausted: the run has spent or reserved its budget. Nothing was reserved by the refused step and its adapter was not called. Raise CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS (a restart applies it) and start a new run; do not edit or delete a reservation row (the database refuses both, and no operator action lowers a charge).
  2. reservation_replayed: this step (run, node, occurrence, attempt) already holds a reservation, so a provider call for it may already have spent. The platform does not call again on that strength. The node's own in-process retry is the next attempt and reserves afresh; if the run has no retry left, start a new run. After a crash or a process-level re-execution the attempt counter restarts at 1, so the resumed governed node is refused with this code and the run fails: a governed step cannot be resumed after a crash, only a new run proceeds (known limit, follow-up #1073). It fails closed: no second provider spend happens under one reservation.
  3. A reservation still reserved: its worker died or was cancelled. It is already counted in full. The execution owner's reconciler loop moves it to abandoned (still at its whole reservation) once its step's deadline plus the grace has passed; if it does not (caliber_worker_heartbeats shows no live effect_reconciler, or the loop is turned off), the row stays open and keeps counting, which is safe. Start the loop by fixing the owner (see Owner crash and failover); do not update the row. A worker that returns after the owner abandoned its reservation cannot lower the charge, and an overrun it reports after that (past the step's deadline plus the grace) is not recorded.
  4. store_failed: the database could not take the reservation (or migration 0133 has not run). Nothing was reserved and the adapter was not called. Fix the database or run the migration, then retry.

Never. Delete or edit a reservation to "give the tokens back". The provider may have charged them.

Callback and webhook redelivery#

The receipt callback (POST /caliber/effects/callbacks/receipt, signed, no session) is the one consumer of the inbound inbox (caliber_inbox_events, key (consumer, source, event_id); consumer effect-callback, the source a digest of the connector and project, the event id the X-Caliber-Delivery header). What each answer means for the sender:

AnswerMeaningThe sender should
200 status: duplicatethis delivery id was already consumed with this key; nothing appliedstop: it succeeded earlier
200 status: already_committedthe proposal is committed (a new delivery id, or it lost a race to the commit)stop
200 status: committed with receipt_idrecorded nowstop
202 status: unknownthe downstream holds nothing (yet) under the key, or something that is not this effect; nothing consumedtry again later with the same or a new delivery id
202 status: in_flightstill dispatched: the dispatcher, or the reconciler once abandoned, owns ittry again later
409 inbox_payload_mismatchthe same delivery id with a different keysend the new message under a new delivery id; never reuse an id
409 with a reason code (receipt_conflict, stale_version, ...)the commit was refused and rolled back whole, the reservation tooretry the same delivery
409 proposal_failed, not_dispatchedthe proposal is failed, or was never dispatcheddo not retry; it is not waiting for a receipt
502 lookup_failed, 503 busythe downstream could not be asked (or four lookups for this connector and project are in flight)retry
404 no such proposalnot this connector's, not this project's, or no such keycheck the key
401 callback rejectedunknown connector or project, unreadable secret, bad signature or a timestamp more than 300 s off: one answer for allcheck the binding, the secret and the clock

A delivery answered 5xx, or never answered because the process died before the commit, left no reservation: the sender's retry is processed. A failed transaction is never treated as already processed.

An inbox row stuck at received. A reservation and its processed marker commit in one transaction, so a committed received row can only come from an apply that committed or rolled back the session it was handed (InboxContractError). Every later delivery of that id is then answered duplicate. Steps:

  1. List the rows (query above) and note the consumer, source, event_id.
  2. For effect-callback, the proposal's own state is the truth: read it in the view by logical_key. If it is committed, nothing is lost; if it is unknown, ask the connector to send the callback again under a new delivery id (a new id is a new inbox key, so it is processed and the platform asks the downstream again).
  3. Do not edit or delete the row. Report it with the row and the proposal state: it indicates a defect in the consumer.

The GitHub webhook is not a consumer of this table. It has its own signed delivery inbox (caliber_workspace_source_events): a repeat delivery is 202 with duplicate: true and no second row, and a reused delivery id with different evidence gets the same generic 401 as any other rejection (deliberately not a 409). Nothing to recover; the sender's retry is safe.

Outbox backlog and dead letters#

Business events (the outbox). Run events are written to caliber_event_outbox in the transaction of the transition that caused them, then delivered by OutboxPublisher, an owner-only loop. Delivery is at least once; consumers deduplicate on (consumer, event_id). Read the depth with the query above, or from Python:

import os

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

from caliber.events.outbox import outbox_depth

factory = sessionmaker(create_engine(os.environ["CALIBER_DATABASE_URL"]))
with factory() as session:
    # {"pending": ..., "delivered": ..., "dead": ..., "oldest_pending": ...}: the last is the creation time of the
    # oldest row that is still pending, the lag of the slowest undelivered event
    print(outbox_depth(session))
You seeCauseDo
pending grows, oldest_pending is old, no ownerthe publisher runs only on the lease holderOwner crash and failover
pending grows with an ownera consumer keeps failing; last_error names the consumer and the exception class, never a message or payloadfix the consumer; rows retry with exponential backoff (cap 300 s)
dead rowsa row ran out of CALIBER_EVENT_OUTBOX_MAX_ATTEMPTS (default 20), or every earlier handoff attempt never finished (abandoned: ...)keep them: they are the record. There is no replay tool yet; report the rows with event_id and last_error

Delivered rows are pruned after CALIBER_EVENT_OUTBOX_RETENTION_DAYS (7); dead rows are never pruned. The default registers no consumer, so a healthy default deployment shows pending near zero and no growth in dead.

Outbound webhooks (dead letters). An event the dispatcher could not deliver is recorded in caliber_webhook_dead_letters, with a kind: exhausted (the receiver is broken), overflow (CALIBER shed load), shutdown (accepted and still queued when the owner stopped or died) or accept_failed (the database could not record the acceptance, so the event was deliberately not sent).

  1. GET /caliber/system/webhook-dead-letters (defaults to status=open).
  2. Fix the receiver first. Delivery is at least once by design, so a receiver must tolerate a repeat.
  3. POST /caliber/system/webhook-dead-letters/{dead_letter_id}/replay (operator). A replay that fails leaves the row open with the reason; two concurrent replays are arbitrated by the database (the loser gets 409). 503 means no dispatcher is configured or delivery is disabled.
  4. For an event that must not be sent: POST .../acknowledge with a note. It marks the row handled; it deletes nothing.

Nothing redelivers a dead letter by itself, and a replay is a new send: do it only when the receiver is healthy.

A run refused for its pins or its rule bundle#

A run admitted in the reference profile executes exactly what its manifest pinned, and fails closed when that is no longer true. Two different things happen, and they are told apart by where you see them. These are explained, with every code and its recovery, in Reference profile; the short version for the operator.

Refused at admission (no run is created; the HTTP 409 body carries only a message, not a code, so match the message text):

The messageRecovery
"this workflow version has no sealed deployment bundle", "failed its integrity check", or "unresolved dependencies" (internally bundle_unavailable)compile and publish the version again
starts rule_bundle_refused: (internally a manifest refusal)restore the bundle file or update the pinned digest deliberately (path and digest together)

A run that ended failed (the run has an error code and a summary):

The run's error codeRecovery
pins_changed, pins_mismatch, model_route_changedthe run stays failed; restore what changed or submit a new run
context_denied, the summary naming rule_bundle_changed or rule_bundle_unavailablethe run stays failed even if you restore the file; resubmit
authority_denied (grant_expired, grant_revoked, not_a_member)submit a new run as someone who may

The same rule as for effects applies: a refused run is not resumed, and a new run is a new run. For a run that had an effect in doubt, settle the effect first (A gated, parked, or failed run).

After a restore#

Backup and restore are in Backup and recovery: back up the CALIBER database and the MLflow backend store together, restore the secret encryption key separately, run caliber-migrate against the restored database, then verify /readiness reports ready: true including the schema check, and run Reconcile releases on the Releases page. The effect, receipt, manifest, outbox and inbox tables live in the CALIBER database and are restored with it, back to the snapshot time. What that means for effects, which that page does not cover:

  1. Stop every replica before you restore.
  2. Start the restored deployment with CALIBER_BACKGROUND_TASKS_ENABLED=false: no loop runs and every replica is a secondary (there is no lease to take), so nothing executes yet.
  3. Compare the downstream with the runs and effects created after the snapshot time. An effect made after that point has no ledger or proposal row in the restored database, and a restored queued or running run will perform it again. The restored lease row and every dispatch_token are from snapshot time too, so a restored token can be lower than tokens issued after it.
  4. Only when that comparison is done, enable background tasks again.

Do not hand-edit rows to reconcile them with the downstream; use the sections above.
